title: The relentless math of bandwagoning
content:
It often seems that everyone is talking about what everyone is talking about.

No one cares about a song or a movie or a political issue–and then they do. Then it’s everywhere.

But of course, that’s precisely why. Most people feel safe when they’re engaging within the expected social norms. It’s easier to fit in and to avoid an error. Or, if that’s your thing, it’s easier to stand out in contrast to everyone else who is trying to fit in. Either way, we’re always on the lookout for a bandwagon to hop on.

The media, in their relentless search for newsstand sales, clicks and likes, seek precisely the same thing. PT Barnum figured out that putting a marching band on a wagon at the front of the parade drew a crowd, and then Dan Rice, an actual clown, realized that politicians would be eager to ride on a wagon that had a crowd, which drew others to the crowd and the cycle continued.

The math is simple: you can’t bandwagon by yourself. The nature of bandwagoning means that it will always be overrepresented in any sampling of the media.

Just because someone organized a parade doesn’t mean you have to be in it.

title: Forensic Facial Specialists Can Identify People Using Just a Couple Facial Features
content:
Artificial intelligence is already being used for facial recognition, but how good is it?

In lab conditions, it’s extraordinarily precise, correctly identifying people 99 percent of the time. In the real world, however, things get a little tougher. Bad lighting, sunglasses, clothing, and more can either flummox AI facial recognition systems or lead to false positives. Of course, we already have human forensic facial specialists, and a better understanding of their expertise could help train their computer counterparts.

**Read more: “[Get Ready to Be Identified by Your Ear](https://nautil.us/get-ready-to-be-identified-by-your-ear-236058)”**

To investigate, a team of cognitive and AI researchers from the National Institute of Standards and Technology recruited 27 forensic facial experts employed by the federal government. The specialists were given images of two similar faces and one hidden face. The goal was to match the obscured face to one of the other faces by individually removing the coverings from nine different features: cheeks, chin, ears, eyes, eyebrows, forehead, neck, nose, and mouth. A points system incentivized the experts to uncover the fewest possible features and another version of the experiment individually uncovered the features at random.

An example of the experiment. One of the two faces matches the hidden face, and the forensic facial specialists have to identify which one by selectively uncovering certain facial features. _Credit: Hahn et al., 2026_

So how did they do?

According to the study [published](http://dx.doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0359520) in _PLOS One_, they were incredibly accurate, correctly identifying the hidden face 90 percent of the time after uncovering only one or two features. “What surprised me most was that specialists could accurately judge identity from a single facial feature most of the time,” study author Carina Hahn said in a [statement](https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/1147692). “It’s remarkable how much identity information they can extract from so little.”

Ears, the team found, were the experts’ favorite feature to uncover (and proved to be extremely useful for identification), but they strategically selected other features next as they adapted. Interestingly, along with ears, the seldom-selected foreheads were associated with the highest accuracy (chins and necks were the least helpful). Taken together, the findings are consistent with other research results, which suggest that certain aspects of our faces contain more identifying information than others.

But the adaptability is what stood out to the team. “Specialists have a striking ability to adapt their strategy depending on the face in front of them, rather than applying one fixed rule,” Hahn explained. “The combination of relying on features known to be useful, like ears, with adjusting when needed, hasn’t been documented before.”

Importantly, the team cautions that this experiment doesn’t mimic real-word conditions, nor is it meant to. Instead the findings may be useful for training both human and AI facial specialists in the future. So if you’d like to avoid AI identification going forward, remember to pack your earmuffs. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Is This the First Corporate Psychopath?
content:
In 1629, the Dutch East India Company ship Batavia set sail for Java in the East Indies, but never made it to its final destination. Instead, it ran aground on the Abrolhos Islands, a chain of small islands off the west coast of Australia. Some 200 souls survived, but soon discovered both food and fresh water were lacking. To compound problems, the ship’s officers absconded in a sail boat pointed toward Java to get help, leaving a power vacuum.

That vacuum was filled by Jeronimus Cornelisz, a junior merchant on his first voyage who had abandoned his wife and child, and his reign was barbarous. According to a new historical case study [published](http://dx.doi.org/10.1007/s13520-026-00274-y) in the _Asian Journal of Business Ethics_, it also bore all the hallmarks of corporate psychopathy—perhaps the first such instance.

**Read more: “[Are You Smart Enough to Avoid Falling for “Corporate Bullsh*t”?](https://nautil.us/are-you-smart-enough-to-avoid-falling-for-corporate-bullsht-1278697)”**

True psychopaths are relatively rare, accounting for only around one percent of the population. In business, they’re a bit more common (conservative estimates put the incidence around three to four percent). According to study author Clive Boddy, a corporate psychopath displays some combination of different abhorrent characteristics: deploying superficial charm to gain trust, surrounding themselves with loyalists, creating a climate of fear, sowing discord among rivals, eliminating challengers, avoiding blame, and pursuing power, money, and control above all else (sound familiar?).

Cornelisz, Boddy says, did a speedrun of the corporate psychopathy checklist during his brief, murderous stint as self-proclaimed “Captain-General” of the island. Planning a mutiny even before the shipwreck, he quickly consolidated power, replacing any other lawful officials with his own mutineers. He demanded loyalty oaths from his freshly minted lieutenants, and his crew started hoarding resources.

Cornelisz then set about dividing his opposition. He tricked one potential rival, a Dutch soldier named Wiebbe Hayes, into leading a search with 20 other soldiers for fresh water on neighboring islands. While Cornelisz evidently believed the quest to be doomed from the start, Hayes located two water sources, organized hunts, and soon amassed enough food to provide for the entire group.

Unfortunately, Hayes’ smoke signals to the main group went unanswered. Back on his own island, Cornelisz was busy killing anyone who he perceived as a threat to his power—over 100 in total—and pressed the few remaining women into sex slavery. According to Boddy, the murder was justified as a way to conserve resources, but functioned as an intimidation tactic and a means to implicate Cornelisz’s underlings in his crimes, “bound together by being beyond redemption and the law.”

“What makes this case remarkable is that when we analyzed Cornelisz using a modern management psychopathy framework, he displayed every major characteristic associated with corporate psychopaths,” Boddy explained in a [statement](https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/1148675). “The same playbook we see in toxic workplaces today appears in this case from 1629. He removed opponents, rewarded loyalists, created fear, manipulated followers and pursued power at any cost.”

So how did this bloody experiment in corporate psychopathy shake out?

Hayes learned of the barbarity from survivors, used ship wreckage to fashion makeshift weapons, and built a small fort on a hilltop. From that fortification he was able to repel at least three assaults by Cornelisz’s forces. Cornelisz was eventually captured, and he was tortured and executed when the ship’s captain returned from Java.

“Perhaps the most striking finding is that another leader facing the same circumstances achieved completely different outcomes. Wiebbe Hayes built cooperation, discovered new resources, and kept people alive,” Boddy said. “This was effectively a natural experiment in leadership. One group prospered while the other descended into murder and abuse.”

It’s just too bad the “first corporate psychopath” wasn’t the last. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: LSD May Speed Up Brain Activity and Make it Fractal
content:
LSD was a relative latecomer to long-established traditions of humans consuming hallucinogenic substances. But in a linguistic sense, it was the first psychedelic. In 1956, British psychiatrist Humphry Osmond coined the term “psychedelic” to describe LSD’s intoxicating effects in correspondence with writer Aldous Huxley. Those who ingest the drug can experience kaleidoscopic visual patterns, a temporary dissolution of self, a slowing or stopping of time, and wild shifts in mood that can range from deep euphoria to severe anxiety and confusion. “To fathom Hell or soar angelic, Just take a pinch of psychedelic,” Osmond quipped in his letter to Huxley.

**Read more:**[**“This Obscure 1960s Guide to LSD Holds Up”**](https://nautil.us/this-obscure-1960s-guide-to-lsd-holds-up-1285476)

Since at least 2012, scientists have [believed](https://www.pnas.org/doi/full/10.1073/pnas.1119598109) that LSD and other psychedelics such as psilocybin alter experience by turning the dial down on activity in the brain’s specific control centers, such as the default mode network, which serves as a central conductor, regulating self-reflection and autobiographical memory and maintaining a sense of ego, or self. More recent research has complicated this idea somewhat, suggesting that connections between some networks are actually strengthened by psychedelics.

But now a small study published earlier this month proposes that LSD may also speed up some key brain rhythms and make brain activity more fractal, with certain patterns emerging and repeating across different timescales. Rather than quieting activity in certain control regions, the drug may also simply alter the background hum. In other words, it’s less that LSD turns off the brain’s controller than that it reshuffles how the whole system talks to itself. The team published their [results](https://www.nature.com/articles/s42003-026-10629-7) in _Communications Biology._

“Imagine a radio station switching its broadcast frequency from 99.5 to 100.5 FM,” said co-author Karim Jerbi, a Université de Montréal neuroscientist and researcher at Mila–the Quebec Artificial Intelligence Institute, in a [statement](https://nouvelles.umontreal.ca/en/article/2026/10/21/lsd-does-more-than-desynchronize-the-brain). “If your radio stays tuned to 99.5, the signal may seem distorted or lost. In the same way, overlooking the shift to faster brain rhythms can lead us to misinterpret LSD’s effects on the brain.” The study was co-authored by Jerbi, together with his doctoral student Venkatesh Subramani and others.

Jerbi and his colleagues re-analyzed the brain recordings of 17 volunteers who either got LSD or a placebo saltwater injection on two separate days. To analyze the subjects’ brain rhythms, the researchers used a technique called magnetoencephalography (MEG), which picks up tiny magnetic fields the brain gives off and can measure changes in that activity over a matter of milliseconds. The volunteers lay quietly with their eyes closed, sometimes in silence and sometimes while listening to one of two seven-minute excerpts from the electro-acoustic ambient album _Yearning_ by Robert Rich and Lisa Moskow.

The team found that LSD sped up the two main rhythms in the brain, known as alpha, which dominates when we’re at rest, and beta, which is linked to focus and decision-making. Using MEG, the researchers found that, in fact, alpha waves sped up by about 2 beats per second, and beta by about 5 beats per second, across large swaths of the cerebral cortex. Older studies had not picked up this change in rhythm because of the way they measured brain activity.

The old method measured only strength: how much total power fell within a specific pre-determined band of frequencies that typically correspond with each type of wave. For instance, in a healthy resting person, alpha waves typically peak pretty regularly at around 10 beats per second—though the exact number varies slightly from one person to the next. The new method separated each rhythm from background static and measured both how fast the frequency was moving, and how strong it was at the peak.

Jerbi and his colleagues also found that the so-called background “hum” of the brain, in which slower frequencies are naturally louder than fast ones, got flatter: Activity became more evenly spread out across speeds, resulting in a less organized signal. But the brain’s overall activity got more complex, more fractal, and less predictable, as measured by the number of distinct patterns showing up in the signal and how many variations occurred in the signal across time. These fractal patterns are found across nature, and echo the kinds of visual patterning that many people taking the drug experience, in which tiny patterns nest one within another like the geometries of a snowflake.

The fact that fractal patterns were found in the brain signal does not necessarily imply a direct link to fractal changes in vision, said Jerbi. “Our findings lend support to this intriguing hypothesis, but they do not yet confirm it. We measure the fractal structure of brain signals over time, not the fractal structure of the images people perceive.”

The brain activity patterns observed by the researchers were clustered in areas associated with vision, hearing, language, emotion, and imagery, but mostly did not affect regions associated with movement, which is consistent with how the drug changes experience. When a person takes LSD, perception is scrambled, but the basic machinery of movement typically remains intact.

One finding surprised the team: Listening to music did not boost the effects of the drug. If anything the data suggested that in fact, music dampened the effects of LSD: The background hum became more dynamic in the participants listening to music, and complexity declined. One hypothesis the scientists offered is that music can act as an anchor, keeping the brain more organized. But this result didn’t hold up under strict statistical analysis, so it’s more of a hint than a fact.

The patterns the team found seemed to be consistent enough that they could be recognized by AI. They trained a machine learning model to predict which brain recordings came from participants on LSD and which ones were from volunteers given a placebo. The model did reasonably well, with between 68 percent and 82 percent accuracy, depending on the specific feature, such as rhythm scores, background hum activity, and complexity scores.

The authors noted that there are some limits to the findings. The study only looked at 17 people, and the recordings came from an older dataset, re-analyzed with the newer methods. The high-frequency gamma findings could also reflect the fact that muscle twitches can sometimes fake certain brain signals, but the authors say the patterns they found are likely too organized for that.

But if the findings hold up, they suggest that the experience of taking LSD is even more complex than we had previously appreciated, and ultimately that it may change our brains in ways that are directly reflected in perceptual experience. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: We Now Know What Denisovans Looked Like
content:
Of all our ancient relatives, the Denisovans might be the most mysterious. While fossils from these archaic hominins were unearthed nearly half a century ago, they were only determined to be a genetically distinct hominin line in the past 15 years. The name Denisovans comes from the Denisova cave in Russia where some of the first specimens were found. Now a new study [published](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-11132-z) in _Nature_ is putting a face to that name.

A team of paleoanthropologists and geneticists from the Chinese Academy of Sciences investigated a cache of 20 fossils dating to around 130,000 years old that were discovered in Xujiayao alongside tools and various animal remains. When the fossils were excavated in the 1970s, it was unclear which hominin group they belonged to. The team’s proteomic sequencing of collagen peptides revealed a key amino acid substitution unique to Denisovans and not found in humans or Neanderthals.

**Read more: “**[**Archaic Hominin Species Buried Only Their Women**](https://nautil.us/archaic-hominin-species-buried-only-their-women-1282257)**”**

The researchers also performed an extensive morphological analysis of the Xujiayao skulls and jaws as well as the Harbin cranium, a near-complete Denisovan skull. According to the team, the Denisovan’s thick, wide skull cap is reminiscent of _Homo erectus_, the cavity that houses their inner ears resembled Neanderthals’, and the tall sides of their vaulted skulls were akin to those of modern humans.

Prior [research](https://nautil.us/youre-carrying-ghost-dna-from-extinct-hominins-1283291) has revealed that early hominins were rather promiscuous. Denisovans in particular interbred with _Homo erectus_, Neanderthals, and even modern humans. So it’s no surprise these hominins shared similar features. The overall shape of Denisovan skulls, however, were somewhat unique. According to their analysis, Denisovans have a relatively long, shallow skull with a low, sloping forehead, massive brow ridges, and flat cheekbones.

Of course, much of what we know about these enigmatic hominins is still new. As we uncover more fossils and technology and molecular techniques improve, the face of Denisovans may change further. Until then, this is our best glimpse into the past. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: A New Fossil Hints at the Surprising Origins of Snakes
content:
Biologists have long debated snake origins. Did they evolve in the sea, underground, or on land, given that today they inhabit all those environments? Now, an exceptionally preserved Cretaceous fossil found in 2020 west of São Paulo, Brazil, sheds a bit of light on snake origins.

A [study](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-10809-9) recently published in the journal _Nature_ described the fossil of a newly identified, very early snake ancestor species, _Tametara mirim_ gen. et sp. nov., that was about the length of the bottom of a coat hanger. Based on its skull anatomy, the authors suggested that the snake led a burrowing lifestyle.

**Read more: “**[**Snakes Break All the Rules**](https://nautil.us/snakes-break-all-the-rules-1206380)**”**

“From the very beginning, I knew I was looking at a very special fossil because of those unusual characteristics,” said study coauthor Gabriel Sobral from the Natural History Museum in Stuttgart, Germany, in a [press release](https://agencia.fapesp.br/fossil-discovered-in-sao-paulo-reveals-new-clues-about-the-origin-of-snakes/59337). “As the work progressed, _Tametara_ revealed itself to be truly unique.”

Led by Princeton University, researchers from the United States, Finland, Brazil, Argentina, and Australia analyzed the fossil, whose estimated age is 85-75 million years. They used high-resolution micro-CT scans to map the contours of its cranium in enough detail to reconstruct its neuroanatomy, including its inner ear, cranial nerves, and brain.

The 3D reconstructions revealed that the ancient snake had dense, overlapping cranial bones, a helmet-like feature found in many species of burrowing animals that protects their skulls from impact. _Tametara_’s eyes likely weren’t great, based on its poorly defined optic lobes—as indicated by the fossil’s brain case—a characteristic typical of animals living in dark places. Its ears also probably functioned like those of a burrower. “The reduced semicircular canals indicate that the animal’s spatial orientation isn’t critical for its perception,” explained Sobral, “which makes sense when living underground.”

The researchers dubbed the new snake _Tametara mirim_ after two words in the indigenous Tupi-Guarani language of the region: _Tametara_ means “adorned” and refers to the crest that tops the skull, and _mirim_ means “small-sized.” Another ancestral snake species that lived during the Cretaceous in what is now Argentina—_Dinilysia_—was determined to be terrestrial but not burrowing, showing that at this relatively early stage in their evolution, snakes had already diverged into distinct habitats that required unique adaptations.

While the discovery of _Tametara_ doesn’t completely resolve the matter of which habitat—subterranean or terrestrial—gave rise to modern snakes, it did show that snakes had already been around for a while, evolving along different paths, by the time _Tametara_ burrowed in the soil about 80 million years ago.

Both _Tametera_ and _Dinilysia_ were extinct by the time modern snakes slithered their way onto the scene. But the two ancient species show that snakes were experimenting with lifestyles early on in the group’s evolution. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Watch Humpback Whales Team Up With Sea Lions to Hunt
content:
It’s not quite on the same level as Timon and Pumbaa or Marlin and Dory, but marine scientists have discovered a fascinating partnership between humpback whales and sea lions in Monterey Bay, California.

The reason for the teaming up, you can probably guess: more food.

Both humpback whales and sea lions go after northern anchovies, but whereas the sea lions chase these fish individually, humpback whales like to charge at large groups of them and swallow as many anchovies as they can at once.

**Read more: “[Humpback Whales Grieve for Lost Offspring, Video Evidence Shows](https://nautil.us/humpback-whales-grieve-for-lost-offspring-video-evidence-shows-1285114)”**

Recording video of several thousand feeding events between 2014 and 2023, researchers found that when sea lions and humpback whales were working together, the sea lions rounded up fish into tighter, denser “bait balls” for the humpback whales to then lunge at. In return, the sea lions circled around their humpback whale friends after each lunge, picking off anchovies already reeling from the whale attack.

Check it out:

[Video 4](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/2026/10/rstb20250344_si_002.mp4)
The research team, which [published](https://doi.org/10.1098/rstb.2025.0344) their findings in the _Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences_, noticed that with the sea lions around, the humpback whales had shorter run-ups to their lunges, spent less time waiting between lunges, and attacked more quickly. However, the energy expenditure and actual “gulp” time stayed the same.

There were no signs of competition between humpback whales and sea lions, or any extra maneuvering from the whales when the sea lions were around—most likely because they both benefit from the arrangement.

That said, the extent of the partnership isn’t clear. The scientists aren’t sure whether the humpback whales are actively following the sea lions around in search of some assistance, or if both species just happen to be in the same area, after the same fish, quite often.

There are, of course, several of these partnerships in the animal kingdom. The researchers highlight as an example the deal between dolphins and seabirds: Dolphins push fish up toward the surface where they can be more easily snatched. Any fish that panic and try to swim back down get gobbled up by the dolphins.

It’s nice to see such teamwork in action. Unless, perhaps, you’re a fish. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: San Francisco Meetup This Saturday
content:
**Why:** We’re having [our usual round of fall meetups](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/meetups-everywhere-2026-times-and), and San Francisco is one of them. I’m signal-boosting this one because it’s likely to be our biggest, and because I plan to be there. I’ll do a Q&A if the sound system is up for it.

**When:** Saturday, October 24, 1 PM to late afternoon

**Where:**[Mox](https://moxsf.com/), 1680 Mission St, San Francisco, CA 94103. Please [RSVP here for the door code](https://www.lesswrong.com/events/huiWRwyZhoF7m6qva/acx-everywhere-fall-26), we will work to make sure people without the code still get in but it’ll be quicker and more reliable if as many people as possible have it.

**Who:** Anyone who wants. You don’t have to pay money or know anything about the blog. Please feel free to come even if you feel awkward about it, even if you’re not “the typical ACX reader”, even if you’re worried people won’t like you, etc. You’re unlikely to be an outlier, regardless of whether you’re very weird, very normie, or somewhere in between.

Anyone who is caught expressing policy opinions will be herded into a side room and made to help create a San Francisco [voting guide](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/ballots-everywhere-times-and-places-673); if you expect this to be you, consider bringing your laptop or ballot materials.

title: Why Global Trepanation?
content:
A friend asked me to investigate the following mystery: why do [5-10% of skulls](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4427816/) from 10,000 BC to 3,000 BC, all over the world, have holes in them? Why do bone growth patterns indicate that most skull-hole-havers survived years after their holes were drilled, even though brain surgery today requires careful sterilization (and frequently, prophylactic antibiotics) to prevent fatal infections? And why did everyone stop doing this sometime around the beginning of recorded history?

Was it cultural diffusion? No. Trepanation (the technical term for drilling a hole in the skull) was common across Europe and South America, with scattered cases in Africa and other continents. The Old and New Worlds had limited contact after about 10,000 BC, and most customs don’t survive for five thousand plus years with no reason.

Was it good medicine? Sort of, but not in a way that entirely solves the mystery. Trepanation is [an effective treatment for](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epidural_hematoma#Treatment) epidural hematoma: a patient ruptures a blood vessel in their skull, filling the cranial cavity with blood, and the pressure rises so high that it squashes various vital blood vessels and brain regions, killing the patient. Drilling a hole in the skull releases the blood, relieves the pressure, and saves the patient’s life. This is great, but these kinds of hematomas are very rare today: about 1/100,000 per year.

So how do you get 5-10% of people trepanned? I think there are two reasons. First, prehistory was [very violent](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-018-0696-8). People were frequently hunting ferocious animals and murdering their friends in tribal quarrels. Epidural hematoma is 1/100,000 in our modern society where people almost never hit their next-door neighbors with flint axes. In a prehistoric culture where people hit their next-door neighbors with flint axes all the time, you presumably get hematoma rates far beyond any in recorded history.

But a 5-10% hematoma rate is still outside any plausible amount of axe-hitting. And although more men than women were trepanned, there were still a lot of trepanned women, even though they were presumably staying out of these quarrels. And although some trepanned skulls show head trauma, others don’t. So there must have been something else going on.

I think the second reason is overgeneralization. Many different cultures observed that trepanning sometimes worked for hematomas. These cases were rare, but they were very dramatic: a comatose person on the edge of death suddenly woke up and felt fine. The prehistoric people who observed this didn’t know what a hematoma was, so they came up with some other explanation (classically “it lets out the evil spirits”). Then they tried the same procedure for other ailments, [just in case](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4427816/) they were caused by the same sort of evil spirits that caused hematomas. Having generated this hypothesis, the usual placebo effect and occasional coincidental recovery ensured that they kept doing it.

(5-10% of people _do_ get migraines; if you already know that drilling a hole in the skull to let the evil spirits out works sometimes, it probably feels pretty tempting when you’re several hours into a migraine attack)

Next question: how did these people survive, when modern brain surgery requires careful sterilization?

Primitive surgeons [drew on](https://libweb.southernct.edu/authors/bibliography/LZ5WSA2J) thousands of years of trepanation experience and stopped at the dura, a layer partway between the scalp and brain. This was enough to relieve epidural hematoma, but stopped short of the most vulnerable and infection-prone areas. They might or might not have been able to examine the dura and determine the rare cases where it was necessary to escalate to a subdural incision, but it wouldn’t have been very often. The scalp has unusually good blood flow, and if you’ve got to make an incision without antibiotics, it’s probably your best bet.

Also, primitive bacteria are weaker than modern hospital bacteria. Modern bacteria have co-lived with large agglomerations of humans for thousands of years; hospital-based variants have gotten transferred from patient to patient by any hospital staff who don’t wash their hands effectively. Wounds that would lead to disaster in modern patients might just not be a problem in the primitive environment.

Why did trepanation stop? The most technically correct answer is that it didn’t; occasional examples survive into historical times, and surgeons use a functionally-similar procedure to relieve hematoma today. But it stopped happening to 5-10% of people, probably because the rate of injuries declined with the advent of civilization. As people got fewer head traumas, there were fewer cases of miraculous recovery, people stopped being so impressed with “letting the evil spirits out” as a cure for everything, and they came up with better placebos like prayer or amulets or resveratrol.

When did the Western world give up belief in the classical good-for-everything version of trepanation? I can’t tell for sure, but it seems to have been sometime between 2015 and 2020, which is when the trail goes dark for the [International Trepanation Advocacy Group](https://web.archive.org/web/20070203000629/http://www.trepan.com/), ITAG. According to its founder, Peter Halvorson:

> ITAG is a grass roots organization comprised of people from many backgrounds and races who have experienced the benefits of being [trepanned](https://web.archive.org/web/20061111070200fw_/http://www.trepan.com/people.html). Some of us are willing to present ourselves publicly so that the old stigma associated with making a hole in the skull will be worn down over time. When people say that they need something or other... "like they need a hole in the head", I laugh and think, '...if they could only have the experience themselves.' At age 57, I've been trepanned now for thirty years. I had the unique opportunity to learn how trepanation can improve mental functions back in my twenties when I traveled abroad. In Amsterdam, I met [Bart Huges](https://web.archive.org/web/20061111070200fw_/http://www.trepan.com/barthuges.html), the originator of the scientific concepts of [consciousness expansion](https://web.archive.org/web/20061111070200fw_/http://www.trepan.com/scroll.html). I gave the subject a thorough review. Enhanced brain functions seemed a perfect antidote to the suffering and despair I observed in the world around me. I saw how people settle for less and have diminished expectations as their energy fades; how they lose direction and settle into an identity much smaller than who they really are.
> 
> 
> They speculate about the meaning of life without ever doing much of anything to make their lives meaningful. I wanted none of that suffering for myself. I chose an uncharted course. I managed to get [myself trepanned](https://web.archive.org/web/20061111070200fw_/http://www.trepan.com/peterhalvorson.html) as a young adult. I've seized advantages as they've come my way. I'm committed to my own well being; I've never had a regret about it. You could say I'm a maverick. Through my own trials and tribulations I've been strengthened by the enhanced physiology that's stayed with me. It's there when I'm sleeping. It operates in the background. I find myself busy long after others are asleep. I'm ready to start again early in the A.M. The truth is I can't get enough of life. Some have called it "the fire from within." In mythology it's known as "opening the third eye." For me it's been the energy to stay the course, to persevere, to be the last man standing.

They argue that trepanning increases the volume of blood that can get to the brain. Analogizing it to the fontanelle (the “soft spot” that all babies have in their skull at birth), they conclude that it restores childlike health, creativity, and ability to grow. They [join mainstream medicine](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1173790/) in recommending against self-trepanation, but seem to have found an anonymous Mexican surgeon who would do it for only $2,400. No wonder they got so many volunteers:

[![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!sFSn!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ffd3e6651-9a9a-41be-8d5b-d3332f535ea8_161x267.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!sFSn!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ffd3e6651-9a9a-41be-8d5b-d3332f535ea8_161x267.png)

As late as 2018, the ITAG website (trepan.com) said they were busy trying to do pilot studies to verify their claims. But in 2019, the site went down, and I can’t find any evidence that the organization continues to exist. After over 10,000 years, it seems like this ancient practice is well and truly gone.
